item.title: [heavy.com] Tarik Skubal Makes Feelings on Dodgers Expectations Clear

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, who have their eyes set on a third consecutive World Series title, acquired ace pitcher Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster trade in early August.
In return for Skubal, the Dodgers sent outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith to Detroit.
Right now, it remains to be seen whether or not the Dodgers will be able to re-sign Skubal, who can become an unrestricted free agent following the season, and is expected to potentially command upwards of $400 million on his next contract.
Los Angeles Dodgers Pitcher Tarik Skubal Makes Feelings On Expectations Clear
In an interview with Bill Shaikin of the Los Angeles Times, Skubal said he’s come to embrace the heightened expectations that come with being the reigning American League Cy Young Award winner, and having joined a club with legitimate title aspirations.
“I’ve grown to appreciate expectations from teammates, from fans, from organizations,” he said. “I’ve come to appreciate pressure. Early on in my career, there wasn’t much of that. It was more just kind of finding my footing, which I’m grateful for. It helped me learn a lot about myself.
“Having the expectation of being a team that is going to win the World Series, and me being a part of that, is something that I’ve come to really appreciate,” he continued. “I’ve come to appreciate all that stuff. As much as they can be looked at as negative things, or stress-inducing things, I’ve come to really appreciate those things, because I haven’t had that for my entire career.”
Meanwhile, he discussed his admiration for Clayton Kershaw, who played his entire 18-year MLB career with the Dodgers, winning three World Series rings.
“It takes a superhuman to be held to the standard he was being held to, in the biggest of moments,” Skubal said. “I think he was great. He did everything he could for his team. He wore it out there sometimes. Chasing box scores and stuff is kind of unfair to judge guys on, because I’m sure he was pitching through some stuff and grinding through some stuff.
“But he had to do it, because he was Clayton Kershaw.”
Dodgers Manager Dave Roberts Points To Major Difference Between Los Angeles And Detroit
According to Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, the difference between Los Angeles and Detroit is clear – the goal for the Dodgers is World Series or bust.
“There’s also a difference between being on a team like the Tigers — and nothing against that organization — where the goal really isn’t to win the World Series. It’s the hope,” Roberts said. “But being here and seeing the standard that we have and it’s like: ‘I’m here to win the World Series. This team has the best chance to win the World Series, and I get to be a part of it.’

item.content:encoded:
Cubs rumors: Chicago insider dumps cold water over any potential Tarik Skubal free agency pursuit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Chicago Cubs saw their season comes to an end Wednesday night when they were eliminated from the Wild Card round of the National League playoffs by the San Diego Padres. The Cubs lost the series in consecutive games after earning a spot in the postseason in the final days of the season.
While their time in the postseason was short-lived, the Cubs had multiple winning streaks in the early part of the season that allowed them to challenge the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Central Division. However, the Cubs could not match Milwaukee's consistency throughout the year, and they finished 14 games behind the Brewers.
The Cubs will almost certainly have multiple changes to their roster when the 2027 season gets underway. The Cubs have multiple free agents, including outfielders Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki as well as pitcher Shota Imanaga.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
However, the Cubs are not likely to get involved in the bidding for the top free agent expected to be available. Tarik Skubal of the Dodgers is expected to receive the top contract offer ever made to a pitcher in MLB history.
Skubal was traded by the Detroit Tigers to the Dodgers this summer. Skubal is represented by top player agent Scott Boras, and Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner.
While a number of teams may get involved in the bidding for Skubal, an insider with ties to the Cubs does not believe the team will make a significant bid for the dynamic 29-year-old left-handed pitcher.
The Cubs have already committed about $110 million to future player contracts in 2027.
Related: 1 free agent Cubs must re-sign after losing in postseason to Padres
Related: 3 radical changes Red Sox must make this offseason after humiliating playoff loss

item.title: [North Side Baseball] Don't Stop Him Now: The Breathtaking Brilliance of Pete Crow-Armstrong, One More Time
item.dc:creator: Matthew Trueblood

item.content:encoded:
Cubs Video
It's every human's greatest (if, at times, subconscious or unwanted) wish to be understood—to have others really see us as we see ourselves and grasp what we believe gives life its meaning. The great danger of being a parent lies in either being too successful at imprinting your understanding of the world on your child (thereby passing down to them your biases, your shortcomings and your ossifications of thought, and making a clone of yourself, which will become an ill-adjusted being in a world very different from your own), or in feeling an eternal frustration that grows from the inability to communicate to someone so close that essential self-understanding that must be communicated to bring happiness.
I have always feared the former, more than the latter. I don't want my kids to be too much like me; I try to teach them mostly by pointing out my own mistakes and demanding that they avoid repeating them. Sometimes, though, that internal truth breaks containment, even when we don't want it to. In ways big and small, conscious and utterly accidental, we bare our souls to one another and a certain transference happens, whether we like it or not. In early August 2018, a YouTube user uploaded this highlight video of Javier Báez's season to that point. I loved it. Absent-mindedly, because my 5-year-old liked baseball and wanted something to watch, I showed it to him, too.
It was one of those moments. My son has never been the same; that video rewired his personality. Since then, he's been not only a rabid baseball fan, but a tenacious player—and on and off the diamond, this is the energy he seems to bring to life. It's a relief, in one way, because that's not the energy I bring to life, so he's certainly carving his own identity, but I lose some sleep over the possibility that I've turned him into a demon as obsessed with excellence and domination and creativity as Báez was in his best season, with (surely) less talent to give it all the proper outlets.
When the Cubs traded Báez a few years later, I was sad, and my son was even sadder. Of course, the playstyle on that tape was never going to age especially well, and Báez's more-bad-than-good years since have eased the pain of knowing the Cubs dealt him away, but the joy and ferocity of his game (at its best) was still absent from Cubdom, and the loss was felt, however inevitable I might have known it to be.
Right away, though, my son latched onto Pete Crow-Armstrong. The same sizzling intensity bends the light all around Crow-Armstrong, making him shimmer and raising the temperature (for good and ill) every time he's on the field. I was a bit slower to take the same depth of enjoyment from his game, because some of the rough edges around the game felt less endearing in Crow-Armstrong's case than in Báez's. Once I saw him reinvent himself at the plate (for the first time, way back in mid-2024), however, I was on board. He was adaptable, after all. He was intelligent, after all. He might even be more talented than Báez, and capable of applying that talent a bit more judiciously to his game.
That, of course, is what we've seen over the last two years. It was fun when Crow-Armstrong took off like a shot in 2025 and surpassed 20 homers and 20 steals before the All-Star break, but you could sense the recoil coming, and sure enough, he had a miserable final two months at the plate. The real breakout—the moment he went from a lovable star with two-way value to a generational guy—finally came this spring, as he adjusted to the bat speed he'd added over the offseason and altered his approach. That's when Crow-Armstrong became a player as winning-focused, clutch, and electrifying as Báez had been, although in a different way.
The internet has changed (read: worsened) over the last eight years, and no good analog for that Báez highlight reel is easy to find for Crow-Armstrong. Because everyone is desperately trying to monetize YouTube traffic for themselves, and because viewing hours determine monetization rates and pull in the money, you can watch four-minute highlights from MLB's official channel that include just one at-bat and the ensuing home-run trot, or 25-minute compilations of plays made by simply stringing together the full versions of original 30-second clips, but you won't find sleek, well-produced highlight videos as readily. So be it. I want to offer just one brief set of clips that illustrate the point, as a way of celebrating and remembering the magical season that just came to an end.
There's a big, grandiose way to do this, and maybe we'll do it another time. Today, we're doing the cozy minimalist version. Yes, there were a couple of months early this year when Crow-Armstrong played arguably the best defense in center field that the game has ever seen. Yes, there was a month in which he had an OPS of 1.249. Yes, there was one week in which he almost single-handedly won the Cubs four games, and yes, there were individual games scattered throughout the calendar in which he took the spotlight in ways we've hardly seen before. But I just want to talk about one game, in which he started the day 0-for-3 and the Cubs were slouching toward a 2-0 loss.
The date was August 6, which was supposed to be an off day. Because rain had postponed the team's series finale against the Blue Jays in June, though, Toronto had come back to town on a mutual blank space in the teams' schedules. It could have been a really tough moment in the team's season, but instead, they were riding high. Crow-Armstrong had won them a game against the Yankees over the weekend, and he'd just won them one the previous night against the Dodgers, showing Shohei Ohtani who was boss in the last moment at which anyone wondered which of the two would be the MVP of the National League.
It was a day game after a night game, though, and Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-3 through the first seven innings, with a strikeout. David Peterson pitched well, but gave up one run in the first, and the Jays tacked on a second tally in the seventh. Their near-automatic closer Louis Varland came on to save the game in the bottom of the ninth, with the cushion of that late run making things much less stressful. Crow-Armstrong wasn't even the tying run, when he led off the inning. Varland went right after his superstar opponent, getting ahead 0-2. Then, Crow-Armstrong slammed into one.
This was not one of his most vicious swings. It doesn't look like a case of cutting down with two strikes, but it was that, a little bit. He made sure he would connect solidly, rather than swinging for the fences (as he did for much of the year). The ball half-split the gap, too, and he probably could have had second on the play. Not playing for stats, though, he held at first, knowing his run meant too little to risk an attempt to advance. That set up Alex Bregman's dramatic, game-tying two-run homer, which sent the game to extra innings.
The Cubs should probably have won in 10 innings, but it went to 11. They held Toronto scoreless in the top half of each frame, so when Crow-Armstrong stepped in to lead off the bottom of the 11th, Carson Kelly stood at second base, carrying the winning run. He had a tough assignment, taking on lefty Brendon Little, and Little tried to leverage his platoon advantage. He also tried not to give Crow-Armstrong any chance to win the game for the Cubs—so much so that he threw him neither a fastball nor a strike the entire at-bat.
Every past version of Crow-Armstrong gets himself out in that situation, probably via strikeout. This version, though, showed a well-considered blend of intelligence and aggressiveness. He wasn't going to passively accept a walk. He felt he had a chance to win the game for the team. Nor, however, would he unduly expand his zone and leave Kelly at second with one down. He took two balls and fouled off a few two-strike offerings. Finally, on a 2-2 curveball that didn't dip quite low enough, he hit it right back through the box for a single. It could, even, have been the game-winner.
As it happened, though, Kelly shouldn't even have tried to score. He didn't get a clean enough break from second, and Myles Straw (who has a strong arm and charged the ball perfectly) got off too good a throw. The slow-footed Cubs catcher should have held at third, where a whole lot of possible things might have brought him home to walk it off. Instead, he ran into a pivotal first out.
Crow-Armstrong hadn't been anticipating a celebration or thinking too conservatively, though. The throw came through to the plate and thwarted Kelly, but when it did so, Crow-Armstrong advanced to second. Thus, the winning run was right back in scoring position—and now, it was a guy who was utterly determined to score it.
Few runners try to steal third with a lefty in the batter's box. Pitchouts are vanishingly rare in the modern game, but catchers have a clear lane to make a short throw when a lefty is at bat. All year, the league only attempted 70 steals of third from the seventh inning on. At that moment, in early August, the Cubs had only attempted one such steal all season. Here it is:
Yep, it was Crow-Armstrong, and it came when the situation demanded it—putting him at third with less than two outs, when he carried the tying run in the final inning of the game. In that contest, the Cubs stranded him there and lost; they let Crow-Armstrong down a lot this year. But he hadn't been afraid then, and he wouldn't be afraid this time, either.
This time, things broke just right for Chicago. Crow-Armstrong had the base stolen, anyway, but then the ball trickled away. It didn't even go that far; this was no airmailed ball into the left-field corner. It was enough, though. As soon as it began to roll away, Crow-Armstrong was off toward the plate. He had willed his team to a fourth straight win. It looked like the Summer of PCA might never end.
Baseball doesn't always reward such courage, even when paired with great talent. But the game is at its best when someone has the temerity and the instincts to get a delicate thing like that right. In fact, life is at its best in moments like that, when someone takes a bold chance in the service of both themselves and others and it pays off. The magic of Crow-Armstrong, this year, was distilled as gorgeously in that moment as in any other play he made—in the field, at bat, or on the bases. It felt a whole lot like when Báez scintillated with the same clutchness and fire and unstoppable talent, eight years ago.
I hadn't even initially thought of this, but now that I have, I feel compelled to include it. There was another moment akin to this one, in a way, from earlier in my baseball season—way earlier, back on May 20. It wasn't Crow-Armstrong making this particular play, but I had a better seat for it.
I know I don't want my children's personalities to be as closely wired to sports as mine was when I was their age. I don't know whether I want them to view Crow-Armstrong (whom I have found thoughtful, sharp and generous in my few interactions with him, and whom most people say means well even off the field) as a role model, except in the limited context of the game. However, what Crow-Armstrong has tapped into over the last three seasons in Chicago is the same vein of positive intensity that Báez brought years ago, and the legacy of that kind of intensity—of that level of care put into one's work, with a fierce joy held right at the surface and a focus on how what you're doing serves those around you—is a profoundly positive one. It runs deeper than wins and losses, and it extends even beyond a bitter playoff disappointment. The Summer of PCA will, in some ways, never end, even if there aren't great music videos out there of his highlight-reel plays. Sports fans are edified by consuming this kind of baseball. The benefits might even spill beyond the foul lines.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves are in a win-or-go-home scenario on Thursday night when they take on the Philadelphia Phillies in Game 3 of the Wild Card Series.
Both teams are playing for the right to punch their ticket to the NLDS and take on the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers.
But first, they have to handle their business on Thursday night, and ahead of the matchup, Braves manager Walt Weiss made some notable changes to his starting lineup.
Braves Announce Ronald Acuna Jr. Change
In usual fashion for Weiss, he likes to switch up the top of his order from one game to the next with Drake Baldwin and Ronald Acuña Jr.
On Thursday, Weiss will do that again, moving Acuña Jr. down in the order to the two-hole, while Baldwin will move up and bat leadoff.
Here’s the full Phillies lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Braves 10/1 D. Baldwin C R. Acuña Jr. RF M. Olson 1B M. Harris II CF M. Dubón SS M. Yastrzemski LF A. Riley 3B O. Albies 2B D. Smith DH R. Kerr SP.”
Braves 10/1
D. Baldwin C
R. Acuña Jr. RF
M. Olson 1B
M. Harris II CF
M. Dubón SS
M. Yastrzemski LF
A. Riley 3B
O. Albies 2B
D. Smith DH
R. Kerr SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) October 1, 2026
Looking at Game 3 for Braves
Acuña Jr. is due for a breakout game at the plate after going hitless in his first six at-bats across the first two games. However, he scored the first run of Wednesday’s game in the first inning and has also tallied two stolen bases.
Atlanta will send LHP Ray Kerr out to start the game, while the Phillies will counter with RHP Aaron Nola. Both pitchers could have fairly short leashes depending on their performances early on, and as expected, each team will do whatever it can to advance. That could mean emptying the bullpen if needed.

item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the San Francisco Giants had their season come to an end when they lost to the Los Angeles Dodgers (at home) by a score of 5-1.
The Giants did not qualify for the 2026 MLB playoffs.
Giants Announced Devers News
The Giants finished the season without Rafael Devers, as he was placed on the injured list.
They wrote (via X) on September 13: “The #SFGiants made the following roster moves today: • 1B/DH Rafael Devers was placed on the 60-day Injured List with a core muscle injury. • OF Scott Bandura (#91) contract selected from Triple-A Sacramento.”
After the season, the Giants have now announced an update on the 2018 World Series Champion.
MLB.com wrote (on September 29): “Currently rehabbing in San Francisco and will continue his workouts at home next week. Will be fully ready by Spring Training.”
Before getting hurt, Devers finished the 2026 regular season batting .258 with 144 hits, 37 home runs, 98 RBIs and 88 runs in 148 games.
Looking At Devers
Devers had spent the first 8.5 seasons of his career with the Boston Red Sox.
In that span, he made three MLB All-Star Games.
The 29-year-old was traded to the Giants during the middle of the 2025 season.
The Giants wrote (via X) on June 15, 2025: “The #SFGiants and Boston Red Sox completed a trade today, with IF Rafael Devers joining the Giants in exchange for LHP Kyle Harrison, RHP Jordan Hicks, RHP Jose Bello and OF James Tibbs III.”
Looking At The Giants Right Now
The Giants had come into the year with a notable roster.
That said, they had a tough season under first-year manager Tony Vitello.
After making trades (and dealing with injuries), the Giants (65-97) finished the 2026 regular season as the fourth-place team in the National League West.

item.title: [chicago.suntimes.com] Stinging from playoff exit, Cubs must make sure next year is different: ‘It’s time to look in the mirror’

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] 3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by NLDS matchup with Padres, 2 reasons to be nervous
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas

item.content:encoded:
After sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres have officially punched their ticket to the NLDS, where a matchup with the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers awaits them. It will be the Brewers and Padres' first-ever meeting in the postseason, and there are no two hotter teams in baseball right now. The Brewers and Padres each posted a 18-6 record during the regular season portion of their September schedule, and San Diego added two more convincing wins over the Cubs this week.
While Brewers fans are relieved not to have to deal with the added stress that comes with facing the Cubs in the postseason, the Padres' recent performance undoubtedly has some fans wishing for a matchup with Craig Counsell's squad. That said, for as well as the Padres are playing right now, there are still certainly reasons for Brewers fans to be encouraged by the specific matchup. Let's take a closer look at three of the Padres' weaknesses and how they might come into play in the NLDS.
3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. Question marks remain in San Diego's starting rotation
Heading into the postseason, the Padres' rotation was certainly their biggest weakness. With an elite bullpen and a surging offense, fans were unsure what San Diego would get from their starting staff in October. However, the duo of Michael King and Nick Pivetta, the latter of whom had a limited regular season workload this year due to an early-season elbow injury, dominated the Cubs in the Wild Card series, allowing just one earned run in a combined 10.1 innings. King's seven-inning shutout on Tuesday night did the heavy lifting, but Pivetta certainly impressed on Wednesday night as well.
However, even if King and Pivetta replicate their Wild Card performances in the NLDS -- likely in Games 2 and 3 -- questions remain in regard to the rest of San Diego's starting options. Trade deadline acquisitions Casey Mize, who is currently hurt, and Robbie Ray, who snuck onto the Wild Card roster but didn't pitch, haven't panned out as the Padres hoped they would. Long-time Los Angeles Dodger Walker Buehler also made the Padres' initial playoff roster, and is certainly a candidate to start a game, but his pedestrian 4.63 ERA in 32 starts this year doesn't necessarily scream "postseason starter." Not only will San Diego need King and Pivetta to repeat their incredible Wild Card performances in the NLDS, but they will also need another less obvious postseason starter to step up.
2. Padres' league-average infield defense bodes well for Brewers' offensive approach
The Cubs had an elite defensive unit in 2026, that much was obvious. In addition to Pete Crow-Armstrong's impressive performance in center field, the Cubs' infield of Alex Bregman (who was limited to DH in the Wild Card series due to a freak injury), Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner, and Michael Busch took away a number of would-be base hits thanks to their impressive range and sure-handedness. The Padres, while their infield unit is fine, by no means have the same elite ability to take away ground-ball base hits, and is therefore a better matchup for the Brewers' offense.
Manny Machado remains a strong defender when it comes to Outs Above Average (OAA), but his Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) total tells a different story. Ty France is a solid defensive first baseman, but the duo of Xander Bogaerts and Jake Cronenworth up the middle is below-average in the field. It's an important part of this series because the Brewers rank first in MLB in Batting Average on Balls in Play (BABIP), third in infield hits, and second in bunt hits. In other words, Milwaukee puts a lot of pressure on opposing infield defenses, and the Padres' shaky unit could come back to hurt them in this series.
3. San Diego's offense was far closer to league average for a majority of the season
The Padres' offense is on fire right now. No team posted a higher collective batting average, slugging percentage, or wRC+ than the Padres during the month of September, and only the Brewers scored more runs. Strong final months from Fernando Tatis Jr., Jackson Merrill, France, and Bogaerts led the Padres to these impressive numbers during the month of September, but for a majority of the season, San Diego's offense looked far closer to league average.
From the start of the season to the end of August, San Diego held a collective wRC+ of 98, indicating that their offensive unit was below league average for the first five months of the season. During that stretch, they ranked 20th in home runs and 22nd in runs scored. Their strong final push made their season-long numbers appear far better, but for a majority of the 2026 season, San Diego's offense was not among the best in baseball. That could matter not if the Padres' recent hot streak continues throughout October, but it's important to note this recent performance is the exception, not the norm.
2 reasons Brewers fans should be nervous about their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. The Padres are the hottest team in baseball (aside from maybe the Brewers)
Whether their recent performance is the exception or not, there's no denying that the Padres are one of the two hottest teams in baseball, with their only threat being the team they will match up against in the NLDS. As previously mentioned, the Brewers and Padres finished first and second, respectively, in runs scored during the final month of the regular season en route to MLB-best 18-6 records. The Padres then stymied a strong Cubs' team with two comfortable wins in the NL Wild Card Series.
For the Brewers, who seemingly run into the hottest team in baseball in the early rounds of the postseason every single year, a matchup with the Padres feels like more bad luck. San Diego surged to the top Wild Card spot in the NL, secured a home postseason series, swept said series, and now carries that momentum into the NLDS. That certainly doesn't feel like a fair draw for the best team in baseball, who just completed a record-breaking 103-win regular season. Yes, the Padres have more flaws on their roster than the Brewers, but sometimes all that matters is how a team is playing when the postseason rolls around, to which the recent performance of each of these two teams would suggest fans are in for a competitive series.
2. San Diego is the only team with a better bullpen than the Brewers
The Brewers are heading into the postseason with their bullpen at its best, which is not often the case following the 162-game season. The combination of Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby at the back end, trade deadline acquisitions JoJo Romero and Antonio Senzatela in the middle innings, and multi-inning options like DL Hall, Chad Patrick, and Shane Drohan has Milwaukee's relief corps among the best in baseball as the playoffs arrive.
However, if there's one bullpen group that is better than the Brewers', it's the Padres' ridiculous assembly of relief weapons. Flame-throwing closer Mason Miller and his elite set-up man Adrian Morejon rightfully garner much of the attention, but other arms like Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, who just returned from the 60-day IL, and southpaw Yuki Matsui deserve respect as well. Given the strength of San Diego's bullpen and the question marks in their rotation, the pressure will be on the Brewers to build early leads and take advantage of as many scoring opportunities as possible.

item.content:encoded:
In 1969, the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers — who were the Seattle Pilots for one season — were founded as MLB expansion teams.
Now, 58 short years later, the perennial National League contenders are meeting in the postseason for the first time.
On Saturday, Oct. 3, the best-of-five NLDS will get underway at Milwaukee’s American Family Field with the Brewers’ ace and Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski (16-5, 1.80 ERA) on the hill.
Following a two-game stint in the Cream City, the series will move to SoCal for a pair of contests at San Diego’s PETCO Park. They’re slated to take place:
Game 3
Tuesday, Oct. 6
Game 4
Wednesday, Oct. 7
If you’d like to be there, tickets are available for both high-stakes hypothetical San Diego showdowns.
At the time of publication, the lowest price we could find on tickets for either game was $121 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $99 including fees for the three potential meetings in Milwaukee.
Before this series, the Padres got revenge against the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card round, sweeping MVP hopeful Pete Crow-Armstrong’s club at home after losing to them in three games to open the playoffs last year.
“They’re playing great baseball right now,” San Diego manager Craig Stammen said about his club.
Next up, they have a tall task taking on MLB’s winningest team in 2026.
Oddsmakers project the Brewers are -180 favorites going into the NLDS.
Yet, it should be factored in that San Diego took four of their six meetings over the course of the regular season including a clutch 4-3, eleven-inning victory on Aug. 12.
Is this the year that one of these two clubs finally gets over the hump and returns to the World Series?
While we can’t say for certain we do know that their first-ever postseason meeting with some of the game’s hardest flamethrowers in Misiorowski and Mason Miller should be downright electric.
Don’t miss this one. We just might have an instant classic on our hands.
For more information, our team has everything you need to know and more about the Padres vs. Brewers 2026 NLDS below.
What do tickets cost to see the Padres at home in the 2026 NLDS?
All hypothetical Padres home game dates at PETCO Park and links to the cheapest tickets available are listed here:

| Game 4 Wednesday, Oct. 7 | $132 (including fees) |
How much are tickets for Brewers 2026 NLDS games in Milwaukee?
A complete calendar of all potential Brewers home games at American Family Field and the lowest-priced tickets can be found below.
| Brewers home game dates | Ticket prices start at |
|---|---|

Are Padres tickets available for later rounds?
Starry-eyed fans looking to get ahead of themselves can procure potential NLCS and World Series tickets before the NLDS even begins.
To grab seats for the game of your choosing, all hypothetical Padres playoff tickets can be found here.
How to watch the Padres in the 2026 playoffs
Fans that prefer to watch on the tube, you can catch Padres playoff contests on FOX, which can be found on DIRECTV.
Huge 2026-27 San Diego shows
The Yankees aren’t the only huge attraction in America’s Finest City these next few months.
Here are just five of the biggest acts headed to San Diego in the near future.
• Don Omar
• Gorillaz
Who else is out and about? Take a look at this list of all the biggest artists coming to the Pechanga Arena these next few months to find the show for you.

Since he started his tenure at the Post in 2022, Levy has reviewed a Bruce Springsteen concert and interviewed Melissa Villaseñor of SNL fame, to name a few. item.title: [pinstripealley.com] MLB Playoff Roundup: Alec Bohm’s 10th-inning homer forces Game 3 against Braves
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa. The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the post
item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.title: [The Virginian-Pilot] Bob Molinaro: Rays, Brewers in World Series would be good for baseball
item.dc:creator: Bob Molinaro
item.description: If only this month, root for the small-market Rays and Brewers. A World Series appearance by either or both might weaken the owners’ argument for a salary cap just enough to save next season. An extinct breed: If you’re wondering how many 20-game winners MLB has had this season, stop looking. There are
item.content:encoded:
If only this month, root for the small-market Rays and Brewers. A World Series appearance by either or both might weaken the owners’ argument for a salary cap just enough to save next season. It wouldn’t hurt baseball, either, for Brewers long-limbed right-hander Jacob Misiorowski, he of the 100-plus mph delivery, the most strikeouts and a 1.80 ERA, to be featured on the biggest stage.
An extinct breed: If you’re wondering how many 20-game winners MLB has had this season, stop looking. There are none. Such is the state of the game.
Done and dusted: Just like that, the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong, the presumptive NL MVP with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases, is out of the playoffs after going hitless in two games against the Padres. That’s baseball.
Early services: Sunday’s Commanders-Colts from London is one of six 9:30 a.m. NFL starts from across the Atlantic in the next seven weeks. Far too many. It still is American football, isn’t it?
Disrespect: The Packers have been so listless this season that Fox moved their Nov. 11 game against the Bears from a late afternoon national window to 1 p.m. That’s a very early flex, but still leaves six nationally televised standalone Green Bay games on the schedule. Though not, the way things are going, for long.
No guarantees: The Rams, who some media magpies said could go undefeated, have already dropped two games in addition to losing quarterback sacker Myles Garrett for six weeks due to injury. The NFL is a cruel mistress.
An odd pairing: Nobody should ever underestimate the now 3-0 Chiefs. But a month ago, who could have imagined that the only Week 4 NFL game between unbeatens would include the Raiders?
In passing: This is my annual reminder that the Colts’ helmet is the best-looking helmet in football.
A team effort: Brian Schottenheimer apologized for mismanaging the end of the game against the Ravens, but the systemic blame for the Cowboys’ loss falls on Jerry Jones, who hired an inexperienced, first-time head coach who won’t cast much of a shadow over Jerry’s ego.
Idle thought: The most dangerous place to stand is between Jones and a TV camera.
Par for the course: The only thing the just completed Presidents Cup had in common with the last Ryder Cup were the scattered boorish shouts and chants from the American gallery.
For what it’s worth: It’s premature to assume the Protect College Sports Act will pass the House of Representatives. Or to think that the bill won’t introduce a new set of challenges and problems.
Roundball: NBA camps are open, and while most of the attention is on LeBron joining Philly, don’t sleep on the Heat now that Giannis Antetokounmpo has taken his talents to South Beach.
Great handle: A spectacular game against Alabama on Saturday would further boost the Heisman hopes of Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor, but the MSU player that catches my eye is running back Fluff Bothwell. He’s a cinch to make the All-Name Team.
Bob Molinaro is a former Virginian-Pilot sports columnist. His Weekly Briefing runs Fridays in The Pilot and Daily Press. He can be reached at bob5molinaro@gmail.com.

item.title: [heavy.com] Toronto Blue Jays Star George Springer's Future in Jeopardy After Retirement Speculation
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: There’s no sugarcoating that the Toronto Blue Jays had a rather disappointing 2026 season. The *technically still* reigning AL Pennant winners failed to qualify for the MLB playoffs, and are officially in offseason mode. Perhaps the biggest offseason storyline with the Blue Jays surrounds All-Star outfielder George Springer and his future in baseball. There has been a lot of speculation about whether Springer will retire from the game of baseball, but that decision is likely not on the horizon u
item.content:encoded:
There’s no sugarcoating that the Toronto Blue Jays had a rather disappointing 2026 season.
The *technically still* reigning AL Pennant winners failed to qualify for the MLB playoffs, and are officially in offseason mode.
Perhaps the biggest offseason storyline with the Blue Jays surrounds All-Star outfielder George Springer and his future in baseball.
There has been a lot of speculation about whether Springer will retire from the game of baseball, but that decision is likely not on the horizon until deeper into the MLB offseason.
However, Springer is on the record as being noncommittal about returning to MLB, as his contract has expired and he’s now a free agent.
More MLB on Heavy: Toronto Blue Jays Trade Prediction Lands 2X MLB All-Star Infielder
George Springer Noncommittal About MLB Future
Following the Toronto Blue Jays’ last regular-season contest, here was the message that George Springer sent to the media regarding his future:
“We’ll go into the offseason and I’ll see what happens….I’ll sit down with my wife at the end of this year and we’ll discuss whatever’s going to happen. But I love my family and if that requires me to be with them, I’ll be with them.”
It’s a fair sentiment to make, as Springer needs some time to weigh the massive life decision and what could potentially lie ahead for his career and future.
MLBTR.com’s Mark Polishuk added (about the Springer speculation):
“While he’ll surely draw interest in free agency, Springer’s market will be limited as a 37-year-old who is essentially a DH-only player at this stage of his career. With 13 seasons played, four All-Star nods, almost $200MM in career earnings, and a World Series ring (and a World Series MVP trophy) with the 2017 Astros on his resume, this may be enough for Springer to call it a career and spend more time with his wife and three young sons.”
George Springer is an extremely accomplished MLB player, but after a long list of nagging injuries throughout his career, it makes sense why he doesn’t want to subject himself to that discomfort any longer.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Mets Tasked with 9 Free Agency Decisions This Offseason
If George Springer’s MLB Career Is Over… It Was a Good One…
George Springer has played in MLB for the past 13 seasons (playing with just two organizations).
Across 1571 total games played, Springer carries a lifetime batting average of .265 with 308 home runs, 850 RBI, and 1595 career hits.
Looking at his Baseball-Reference page, it’s hard to see a major statistical hitting category that Springer would like to reach a milestone in.
After a considerable drop in production in 2026, it’s also unclear if the Blue Jays would even want to retain the 37-year-old All-Star, which brings up the idea that Springer may just want to call it quits rather than play for another organization at this juncture in his career.
Either way, his status is still up in the air, but it will be a big storyline to follow this entire offseason.

item.title: [mix1063.com] White Sox pounce early, finish sweep of Astros for first playoff series win since 2005 | Mix 106.3 – Jonesboro, AR

The White Sox used a big first inning and a three-run homer from Chase Meidroth to propel them to a 7-3 win over the Houston Astros on Wednesday to sweep their AL Wild Card Series. “I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them as they’re probably the only ones in this country that believed that they could be in th
item.content:encoded:
By KRISTIE RIEKEN AP Sports Writer
HOUSTON (AP) — From 100 losses to their first playoff series win in two decades, these scrappy Chicago White Sox just keep outdoing themselves.
The White Sox used a big first inning and a three-run homer from Chase Meidroth to propel them to a 7-3 win over the Houston Astros on Wednesday to sweep their AL Wild Card Series.
“I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them as they’re probably the only ones in this country that believed that they could be in this spot,” manager Will Venable said. “And they maintained that belief in the beginning of the season and went throughout the season maintaining that, and they made it happen. So it’s awesome to get to this point.”
It’s the first time Chicago has won a playoff series since beating Houston in the World Series in 2005. Under the direction of Venable, the second-year skipper, and with a letter of support from Pope Leo XIV, the White Sox advanced to face AL Central champion Cleveland in the AL Division Series beginning Saturday in Cleveland.
“It means everything for our fans,” Meidroth said. “They have been incredible all year. So the main thing was getting back to Chicago for some postseason baseball, and so we’re really blessed that we get to do that.”
The White Sox, who lost 100 games in each of the last three seasons, are the only team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth.
The AL West-winning Astros went 81-81 to become the first team to reach the postseason without a winning record. Their recent playoff woes in Houston continued Wednesday as they dropped their ninth straight home playoff game in a ninth trip to the postseason in the last 10 years.
Chicago pounced on the Astros for four runs in the first inning a day after scoring three in the first two innings of a 6-3 win. Houston ace Hunter Brown was lifted after getting just two outs and wasn’t helped by a sloppy defense which committed two first-inning errors.
He was 6-0 with a 2.39 ERA in six career starts against the White Sox before Wednesday’s debacle.
The Astros clawed their way back into it with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve to trail by 1 entering the sixth inning.
AJ Blubaugh, who opened Game 1, and Peter Lambert, pitching on two days’ rest, combined to retire the next 13 batters after Brown exited. Chicago’s next baserunner came when Lambert walked Andrew Benintendi to start the sixth and then walked Tristan Peters.
Bryan Abreu came in, and Meidroth smashed his fifth pitch off the wall in left field to push the lead to 7-3. He yelled on his entire trip around the bases to the delight of a patch of White Sox fans seated near the visitor’s dugout.
“I was looking for something middle up,” Meidroth said. “He’s had my number all year, really good fastball, so I got something middle up and I was able to cash in for the team. So, yeah, that was awesome.”
Houston faced boos for a second game in a row from an unusually thin crowd. It’s a second straight playoff trip where the Astros have been swept at home in the wild card after losing both games to Detroit in 2024.
Now they’ll face an uncertain future with manager Joe Espada’s contract set to expire at season’s end after general manager Dana Brown was fired last month.
“We fought back and we set our goal to win this division and we accomplished that,” Espada said. “We wanted to play deep in October. We came short on that. But just the way our guys stayed together and were able to get this far, extremely proud of our team.”
It was a disappointing series for Houston slugger and AL MVP-favorite Yordan Alvarez, who managed only a single with two strikeouts in eight at-bats in the series.
Altuve’s shot to the seats in left field in the fourth inning got the Astros within 4-3. It was the 28th postseason homer of his career, which is second in MLB history behind Manny Ramirez (29).
“We’re all sad,” Altuve said. “We wanted to go to the World Series and win it. But today is sorrow for the final day of the season.”
The Astros had a shot to take the lead before Meidroth’s homer. They loaded the bases with two outs in the fifth, but Anthony Kay retired Altuve on a fly out to end the inning.
___

item.content:encoded:
October 01, 2026
It feels sort of unexpected, that the Phillies are not only alive, but have some momentum with the third and final game of the NL Wild Card Series in Atlanta set for Thursday night.
Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure.
Before Game 3's first pitch, we have a few Phillies' thoughts we'd like to share:
How are we feeling about Aaron Nola — named Game 3's starter earlier Thursday morning? In his 15 starts prior to last Saturday's bizarre three run first inning and out for the Phillies' veteran, Nola boasted a pretty solid 3.12 ERA which is more in line with the Nola who got a monster free agent contract a few offseasons ago.
He's also got some postseason pedigree. He's started 11 playoff games over the last five Octobers, and his two worst starts actually came during the World Series run in 2022. In six starts since 2023, he has a 3.00 ERA and 3-2 record. Is he better than Zack Wheeler pitching on three days rest for the first time ever? The Phils coaching staff made their choice and it's a reasonable one, if nothing else.
If Alec Bohm is parting ways with the Phillies in a few weeks — his contract is set to expire and the Phillies are likely to let him walk and give top prospect Aidan Miller the chance to start the season at third (or second) in 2027 — he gave Phillies fans a spectacular parting gift.
ALEC BOHM GO-AHEAD HOMER
PHILLIES LEAD IN THE 10TH 🤯 pic.twitter.com/S4wFOFyDq1
By virtue of all three other Wild Card series' wrapping up (more on that in a second), the Phillies have Thursday all to themselves and have moved from a 2 p.m. start to prime time (at 8:15 on NBC).
The Phillies are no strangers to primetime playoff starts — they've had a ton of them over the last half decade. They also play better at night. Their win percentage under the lights (55.5%, 61-49) is better than during the afternoon (51%, 26-25). With some extra time for their pitchers to rest and prepare, this is probably a net positive move for the Phillies.
As we just mentioned, the other three series' ended with a 2-0 sweep. Since the league switched to the three-game Wild Card first round format, teams who win Game 1 are now 24-3. The Phillies have a chance to be the fourth.
Philadelphia also has the chance to be the first team in franchise history to win a playoff series (albeit a short one) after losing a Game 1. They are 0-9 historically when they start a series off with a loss.
Another mark, probably, in the Phillies' advantage column is that they're going up against a Braves team unprepared to send a third starter out there. Lefty reliever Ray Kerr — with an impressive 1.77 ERA this season — is going to start the game, likely to face the lefty-heavy front of the Phillies order (Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber). Perhaps the Phillies should consider splitting these hitters up and having Schwarber bat lead off, with Trea Turner second and Harper third?
After Kerr, it's expected the Braves will go to righty starter Grant Holmes, who has a 3.44 ERA this season. Holmes faced the Phillies four times during the regular season and the Phils' hitters will all have recent recollections of facing him.
The Phillies will see how far they can get behind Nola, but it'll be interesting to see who's the next man in. Will it be Jesús Luzardo who pitched in Game 1? Will they ultimately call on Wheeler (or optimistically save him for an NLDS Game 1)? Can Andrew Painter throw on back-to-back days?

item.title: [royalsreview.com] Picollo says Royals plan to be “aggressive” in acquisitions after disappointing season
item.dc:creator: Max Rieper

Picollo said the team plans to be “aggressive in acquisitions.” But that aggressiveness, he cautioned, should not be confused with a willingness to spend aggressively on the payroll. item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing 93-loss season, Royals president of baseball operations J.J. Picollo said the team plans to be “aggressive in acquisitions.” But that aggressiveness, he cautioned, should not be confused with a willingness to spend aggressively on the payroll. He addressed the media along with manager Matt Quatraro in the team’s annual end-of-year press conference on Wednesday.
The season did not go as planned, with the team stumbling to a 12-19 start by the end of April. Picollo took addressed the slow start by saying “we’re responsible for the performance in April and May.” He did point out the World Baseball Classic kept some Royals players away from the team during spring training, making it more difficult to build team camaraderie. And injuries made it difficult for the team to climb their way out of the hole they had dug.
“We weren’t very good in April, and we weren’t very good in the beginning of May. I can’t sit here and tell you that I know we would have been good in June, July, August, and September, but if we had had those players on our roster and healthy and available, I think we could have made a better run.”
The Royals lost key players like Maikel Garcia and Vinnie Pasquantino early in the year, in addition to having their pitching staff decimated by injuries over the summer. The Royals announced changes to their medical staff, although Picollo denied the injuries were the reason for the moves. He also contended that despite all the adversity, the team has to win.
“That being said, nobody feels sorry for you. You got to go out and win.”
Here is what Picollo had to say about how he plans to address team needs this offseason.
The bullpen
”The bullpen is going to be a focus for us,” said Picollo. “There’s no question.”
Royals relievers had a 5.07 ERA, second-worst in baseball, and a league-worst 6.65 ERA in the ninth inning. The team lost closer Carlos Estévez to injury after his first game, and got disappointing performances from Lucas Erceg and Matt Strahm.
While Picollo expects the team to be aggressive, he added “I don’t want that mistaken for aggressive payroll spending.” He noted that the team was top five in spending on the bullpen over the last three years, but that spending on relievers may not be the solution due to the volatility of their performance.
“We have to look into ways at being more efficient,” he said, adding that they tried to look for that “diamond in the rough” late this year with waiver claims and small deals. They sought pitchers that presented different arm angles and pitches to give hitters varying looks.
“There’s not a clear, definitive answer on how to pull put a bullpen together. But I think the variety of ‘different looks,’ ‘different stuff’ type of relievers is the way we’re probably going to go.”
Back in August, owner John Sherman said he thought the bullpen could be “cobbled” together without spending too much money.
While Picollo highlighted the pitching of Steven Cruz and Nate Pearson down the stretch, the 2027 closer may not be on the roster right now.
“I don’t know if we’ll be able to sit here today and tell you we’ll have a closer. Internally, we don’t think we necessarily have it.”
Daniel Lynch IV, who enjoyed a breakthrough season in the bullpen, will be given a chance to compete for a starting spot next year. Lynch had a 1.96 ERA in 46 relief appearances this year, and a 6.53 ERA in 10 starts.
Starting pitching
Picollo said starting depth was their biggest priority after upgrading the bullpen. He admitted that the starting pitching depth he had amassed before the season was not nearly enough.
“It was as confident as I’ve ever been in starting pitching depth,” he said before discussing the injuries that hit the pitching staff. Cole Ragans, Kris Bubic, Ryan Bergert, and Stephen Kolek all missed significant time this season.
“So we’re never going to take starting pitching for granted.”
Next year’s rotation will feature Michael Wacha, Seth Lugo, and Noah Cameron, but the team will have to figure out who will fill the last two spots. The team expects to pick up the option of Tony Gonsolin, the former Dodgers All-Star pitcher who was signed late in the year and pitched in one game for the Royals. He could compete for a rotation spot along with Lynch, and Randy Dobnak, who impressed with a 3.51 ERA in 15 games.
Offense
As far as the offense, Picollo liked some of the underlying things they did, but ultimately the team did not score enough runs, particularly on the road. The Royals averaged 4.26 runs per game overall, finishing 21st in baseball. That was a slight improvement over their performance in 2025 when they scored 4.02 runs per game, 26th in baseball. But they finished dead last in baseball in runs on the road, averaging just 3.62 per game.
“It’s a combination of things. It’s getting on base at a greater clip. It’s running the bases well. It’s putting the ball in play when you need to with a man in scoring position. A lot is made of batting average with runners in scoring position - for us its more about ‘did you get him in?’”
He confirmed Ken Rosenthal’s report from Tuesday that hitting coach Alec Zumwalt has been reassigned to focus more on minor league development, but Picollo clarified that this was not a reflection of performance, and had been the plan all along. Zumwalt had worked with the current core of Royals hitters in the minors, and had ascended to the big league level with them. The team wants him back working with young minor league hitters, while assistant hitting coaches Marcus Thames and Connor Dawson work with the big league hitters. The Royals will likely hire another assistant hitting coach, but Picollo backed the work of Zumwalt.
“We’re not disappointed with his performance. We think he’s a very good hitting coach.”
The team will look for offensive upgrades in the outfield. Picollo noted the outfield defense regressed this season, despite the fences at Kauffman Stadium being moved in leaving less room to cover. Outfield prospect Carson Roccaforte could be in the mix, although he is left-handed and Picollo noted that the team is already very left-handed heavy.
The team will be “open to any and all ideas” on trades, even if that means trading players on the roster. Picollo added he is not interested in trading players for prospects, given their timeline and expectations to contend.
“We need to add players that help us at the major league level.”
Spending
Picollo said he does not have a specific payroll figure, but noted that ownership has approved additional spending when he has brought forward opportunities worth pursuing.
“I’ve always felt like it’s not my job to worry about the payroll. Our job is to get the most out of whatever we have,” said Picollo, noting there are teams in the playoffs with lower payrolls than the Royals, while many teams that spent a lot are sitting at home.
“I don’t think payroll is indicative of success on the field. I think success on the field comes with knowing your roster and how to get the most out of your roster and that’s our task. That’s what we need to do.”
Sherman said in August that the team is “freeing up some money” the team could invest, with about $30 million expected to come off the payroll with impending free agents.
When asked about potential long-term contracts for Jac Caglianone or Carter Jensen, Picollo deferred, saying that they typically don’t seriously consider such deals until after a player’s second year of service time. Both players just completed their first full season in the big leagues, finishing strong with each hitting over 20 home runs and posting an OPS+ over 120.
The Royals may have to work quickly to address their shortcomings simply because of the looming potential work stoppage. The collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, which could lead to an end to free agent signings until a new labor deal is worked out.
“The aggressiveness in November is going to be important for us, as we expect the entire industry to be fairly busy.”
But it is clear the Royals have a lot do before the next season begins. The Royals entered 2026 expecting to build on back-to-back winning seasons. Instead, they finished with the fifth-worst record in baseball and now face significant questions in the bullpen, starting rotation and outfield. Picollo acknowledged that the fans demand more.
“It’s refreshing to know that our fans have high expectations. We want them to have high expectations, because we gave them reason to have high expectations,” said Picollo.
“With that comes to responsibility of getting it done. I think we feel pressure every year to win.”

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff schedule 2026: Full bracket, scores, times, TV channels to watch every postseason series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
More than seven months after pitchers and catchers reported to spring training, it's time to determine which team will wear the MLB crown in 2026.
Twelve teams reached the postseason bracket, and any discussion about favorites has to start with the two-time defending champion Dodgers. Los Angeles wasn't necessarily dominant during the regular season and enters October with concerns about the health of the planet's best player, Shohei Ohtani, but it has proven unwise to bet against LA lately.
While the Dodgers are in the midst of a dynastic run, neither of the teams that owned the best records in their respective leagues during the regular season — the Brewers and Rays — has won a World Series. Victory would be particularly sweet for either of those fan bases, along with the other postseason entrant without a title, the Padres.
Who will survive the gauntlet to lift the Commissioner's Trophy at the end of October? Here's when and where to watch every game.
Where to watch MLB playoffs 2026
- TV channels: Fox, FS1, TBS, NBC, NBCSN
The 2026 MLB postseason will have a new look for the opening round, with NBC carrying every wild card game on its platforms: NBC, NBCSN and/or Peacock.
After that, the familiar rotation returns. This year's NL playoffs will air on Fox or FS1 while the AL will be on TBS, with the World Series set to air on Fox as it has every year since 2000.
Fans can stream every postseason game except Peacock exclusives with DIRECTV, which offers a free trial to new subscribers.
All games airing on NBC, NBCSN, Fox and FS1 can be streamed with fubo, which also offers a free trial.

item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies sent Jesus Luzardo out to the mound for Game 1 of the NL Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves. They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive. Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies? According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phil
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies sent Jesus Luzardo out to the mound for Game 1 of the NL Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves. They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive.
Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies?
According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phillies have made their decision between Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. The resurgent Nola will get the Game 3 start, as the Phillies hope to clinch Thursday night in Atlanta.
Phillies turn to Aaron Nola for Game 3 vs. Braves
"Hearing Phillies will start Aaron Nola tonight vs. Braves opener Ray Kerr, a lefty," Salisbury reports. "Always subject to change but that's the plan as of this AM."
The Phillies' plan for the winner-takes-all Game 3 of the NL Wild Card series against the Braves will be to start Nola instead of Wheeler on short rest.
While having Wheeler go would've been preferred, if there was ever a time to trust in Nola, it's this season after his second-half resurgence.
As June came to a close, his 6.04 ERA had Phillies fans, rightfully, very concerned about his massive contract going forward.
But his final 11 starts of the 2026 season resulted in an incredible 2.93 ERA. While some luck has gone his way during that stretch, his massive improvement is giving the Phillies enough confidence to turn to him for Game 3.
On the other side, the Braves are reportedly going to start Ray Kerr, a left-handed pitcher, as potentially an opener until they turn the reins over to Grant Holmes.
The Phillies have Wheeler as an option out of the bullpen for multiple innings in Game 3, but ideally they'll ride Nola for as long as possible.
If they could somehow win without pitching Wheeler, that would be the best-case scenario. The same goes for both Jesus Luzardo and Andrew Painter, both of whom would be willing to pitch in Game 3 if needed.
With how shaky the bullpen is, the Phillies are really going to need Nola to go deep into this game, unless the Phillies' offense comes alive and blows this game out of proportion, and some normal relievers can come into the game without worry of blowing it.
But the most important thing is how Nola performs, as he's expected to get the ball to start the game. It's the right call, especially considering how he's on normal rest and is more ready to go than any other pitcher on the roster.
